clinicalPearls: Presents as a small, bright cherry-red to violaceous dome-shaped papule, most numerous on the trunk of middle-aged and older adults.
Lesions are usually multiple and increase in number and size with advancing age; they are among the commonest acquired vascular proliferations.
Diascopy shows only partial blanching because the vascular spaces are relatively fixed, distinguishing them from simple telangiectasia.
Dermoscopy reveals well-demarcated red or red-blue lacunae separated by pale septa, confirming the vascular nature.
Traumatised lesions may bleed briskly or thrombose, turning dark and mimicking a melanocytic or vascular malignancy.
An abrupt eruption of numerous lesions has been associated with pregnancy, certain chemical exposures and some drugs, though most cases are idiopathic.
No treatment is required; electrocautery, laser or shave removal is used for cosmetic reasons or recurrent bleeding.
A rapidly enlarging or atypical solitary vascular papule should be biopsied to exclude amelanotic melanoma or other malignancy.
reference.pathophysiology: Cherry angiomas are benign proliferations of dilated post-capillary venules and capillaries within the papillary dermis, lined by flattened endothelium and often accompanied by dermal oedema and collagen homogenisation. Increased local expression of angiogenic factors and somatic mutations affecting the GNAQ and GNA11 signalling pathway have been implicated in their development. Their strong association with ageing, and reported clustering during pregnancy or after certain chemical and drug exposures, points to hormonal and environmental modulation of cutaneous angiogenesis. The lesions are stable, non-involuting vascular hamartomatous proliferations without malignant potential.
additionalInvestigations: clinical photography for monitoring multiple lesions
excisional biopsy of an atypical or rapidly changing lesion
review of medication and chemical exposure history in eruptive cases
redFlags: a rapidly enlarging or ulcerated solitary vascular lesion raising concern for amelanotic melanoma or angiosarcoma
an eruptive shower of angiomas prompting review of drug and chemical exposures
persistent bleeding uncontrolled by simple pressure
atypical dermoscopic features lacking the characteristic lacunar pattern
reference.prognosis: Cherry angiomas are entirely benign and persist indefinitely without malignant transformation. Cosmetic removal is generally curative, though new lesions continue to appear with age.
pitfalls: Mistaking a thrombosed cherry angioma for a melanocytic lesion because of its dark colour.
Attributing an eruptive crop solely to ageing and overlooking a drug or chemical trigger.
Assuming any red papule is benign and missing an amelanotic melanoma or pyogenic granuloma.
Inadequate haemostasis during removal leading to troublesome bleeding.
management: Reassurance that the lesions are entirely benign vascular proliferations with no malignant potential, so no treatment is required
Cosmetic removal for unwanted or bothersome lesions by electrodessication, laser such as pulsed-dye or KTP, or shave excision
Haemostasis with cautery for traumatised or briskly bleeding lesions
Excisional biopsy and histology of any atypical, rapidly changing or thrombosed lesion to exclude a vascular or melanocytic malignancy
Review of medication and chemical exposure history where there is an abrupt eruption of numerous lesions
Advise that new lesions commonly continue to appear with advancing age
